sites.name: Tel Shiqmona: purple-dye industry and seasonal production
sites.subtitle: Iron Age coastal industrial compound with purple dye, oil processing, weaving and livestock activity · new peer-reviewed microarchaeological analysis, 2026
sites.date_basis: Excavation stratigraphy and ceramic chronology, supplemented by sediment micromorphology and chemical and micro-remain analysis
sites.location: In situ, Tel Shiqmona, Haifa coast, Israel
overview: Tel Shiqmona preserves an unusually well-documented Iron Age complex with evidence of purple-dye manufacture, olive pressing, textile work and livestock management.

A 2026 PLOS ONE study recovered detailed sedimentary traces of changing use of industrial space. Its proposed seasonal timetable is an interpretation of the archaeological record, not a calendar directly inscribed at the site.
evidence: Purple-stained vessel fragments, murex shells, olive-press installations and loom weights occur in the industrial sequence.
Microscopic sediment evidence includes dung-related spherulites and wood ash, documenting activities beyond purple dye.
questions: The exact season in which the purple-dye workshops operated has not been established directly.
Whether the site's political administration can be attributed to specific named kings is unresolved by these finds.

biblical.tie: Historical context: northern kingdom; no named figure identified at this site
Material setting of eighth-century elite industry; not direct proof of these verses

sources.cite: Ogloblin Ramirez et al., PLOS ONE 21(9): e0355104 (24 September 2026)
Shalvi, Oxford Journal of Archaeology (11 September 2026)

sites.name: Ophel: monumental Second Temple ritual-bath complex
sites.subtitle: Three large mikva’ot, a plastered pool, paved plaza and water system near the Temple Mount · announced September 2026
sites.date: Late Second Temple period, first century BCE–70 CE; announcement 24 September 2026
sites.date_basis: Architectural sequence, associated ceramics and coins; excavation directors' preliminary report
sites.location: In situ, Ophel, immediately south of Temple Mount, Jerusalem
overview: Hebrew University excavations led by Uzi Leibner and Orit Peleg-Barkat exposed a large purification complex immediately south of the Temple Mount.

Three substantial ritual baths, a central plastered pool, a plaza and water installations indicate infrastructure suited to ritual washing. Use by pilgrims is a strongly supported site interpretation, not the identity of particular biblical visitors.
evidence: One bath survives unusually high, including a stone-vaulted ceiling.
Architectural and coin evidence associates the complex with the final centuries of Second Temple Jerusalem.
questions: The precise function of the central pool and traffic patterns through the complex require continued analysis.
Architectural interpretation does not identify individual people or confirm a specific gospel episode.

biblical.tie: Temple pilgrimage setting, not identification with any specific visit
Historical context of Temple purification practices

sources.cite: Leibner and Peleg-Barkat interview, Jerusalem Post, 24 September 2026

sites.name: Mount Scopus: stone-vessel manufacturing workshop
sites.subtitle: Workshop with hundreds of chalkstone fragments, unfinished vessels and production debris · reported February 2026
sites.date: Late Second Temple period, approximately first century BCE–first century CE; reported 20 February 2026
sites.date_basis: Typology and manufacturing remains from a cave workshop
sites.location: Cave on eastern slopes of Mount Scopus near Jerusalem; finds reported by Israel Antiquities Authority
overview: Archaeologists identified a chalkstone vessel-production workshop in a cave east of Jerusalem after an investigation of antiquities theft.
Unfinished stone cups and bowls, waste fragments and lathe-turning marks document a production technique in Jewish society during the late Second Temple era.
evidence: Hundreds of fragments and production debris, together with unfinished forms, support workshop identification.
Turning marks on vessels document use of rotary shaping methods.
questions: The actual buyers and distribution network are not individually documented.
The workshop is contextual evidence for stone vessels, not a discovery of the six jars described in John.

biblical.tie: Stone purification jars are described in this passage; these are not those specific jars

sources.cite: Lauren K. McCormick, Biblical Archaeology Society, 20 February 2026, reporting IAA discovery

sites.name: Pilgrimage Road: Hebrew commercial inscription
sites.subtitle: Small inscribed limestone slab with names and numerical amounts from Jerusalem's Early Roman-period commercial district · discussed July 2026
sites.date: Early Roman period, approximately 37 BCE–70 CE; published/reported 2026
sites.date_basis: Paleography and parallels; recovered from an old excavation tunnel, not original deposit
sites.location: City of David / Pilgrimage Road excavation, Jerusalem; modern repository not verified
overview: A fragment of an inscribed chalkstone slab records portions of Hebrew personal names and amounts, likely a receipt or payment instruction.

Its discovery near Jerusalem's monumental stepped street illuminates commercial exchange in the Second Temple city. Because it came from a nineteenth-century excavation tunnel, it lacks its original depositional context.
evidence: Seven partly preserved lines contain Hebrew letters and numerical signs; a fragment of the name Shimon is legible.
Letter shapes and comparable inscriptions support an Early Roman-period date, despite the disturbed context.
questions: The transaction, full names, precise date and original location of use cannot be securely reconstructed.
There is no evidence identifying the named Shimon with a New Testament individual.

biblical.tie: Commercial activity in Jerusalem offers broad historical context, not direct verification of this scene

sources.cite: City of David / Israel Antiquities Authority report, 26 July 2026, summarizing Szanton and Eshel in ‘Atiqot
